_changelog: v1.0.1 (2026-10-06) review fixes: the coldCase model no longer says the security group is almost certainly the cause, because an office firewall that blocks outgoing knocks on 8080 also times out and AWS's troubleshooting guide (source 2) says to check a corporate firewall; it now says most likely the security group or the office's own firewall, and to test from another network to tell them apart, and coldCase keyIdea 2 widens to match; realWorld[1] adds the guide's corporate-firewall step; the sim gains a Restart button that relaunches the start-up list in a seeded random order, so the race in option B can be played, and a toggle that takes Hal's v1 off the start-up list; sim.tryThis mentions both
title: Knock Knock

post.author: u/dell_after_hours
post.title: I clean an empty office at night and knock before every door. Tonight one of them answered as a man who left two years ago.

blocks.text: I clean the ninth floor of a freight office, ten at night to six. It's always empty. I still knock on every door before I go in. Old hotel habit.

Rosa, the company's only programmer, works days. She once explained her job with my own habit. The big screen by the lifts, where the 5 AM drivers read their pickups, is a client: a program that knocks and asks for something. What answers is a server. Not a machine, she said. A program waiting behind a numbered door on the box in the back closet. The doors are called ports. Web pages live behind door 80, or 443 for the locked kind. Door 22 is for logging in from far away. Door 5432 is the database. The order board is door 8080.

Three weeks ago she replaced Hal's old board program with her own, v2. Hal wrote the first one and left two years ago. At 1:12 AM tonight I plugged the floor polisher into the closet socket and tripped the breaker. When the power came back, the box started up again. Rosa logged in from home and sent me the last line her program wrote before it quit:
01:12:31  board v2  Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::8080

"Something already holds door 8080," she wrote. "Knock on all of them from my laptop." One command knocks on a door and waits up to 5 seconds. A firewall, a guard in front of the doors, ignores outsiders on some of them, she warned. And the database only answers knocks from inside the box itself, from the address called localhost, 127.0.0.1. Here is what I got:

01:40:12  door 443   answered    2 ms
01:40:13  door 80    refused     1 ms
01:40:14  door 5432  refused     1 ms
01:40:15  door 22    no answer, gave up after 5 s
01:40:21  door 8080  answered    2 ms   GOOD NIGHT, HAL

*Refused* came back at once, like someone calling *nobody here* through the door. Door 22 just swallowed the knock. Then 8080 answered, with the greeting Hal's board used to show on night shifts. Hal hasn't worked here for two years. Rosa's v2 never once said that.
Something behind door 8080 still answers as Hal.
Rosa needs the right board up before the drivers walk in at five. What should she do? I'm not knocking on 8080 again tonight.

blocks.label: knocks.png

diagram.aria: Dell's knocks at 1:40 AM, from his laptop, through the firewall, to five doors on the box at 192.0.2.40. Door 443 answered in 2 ms. Door 80 and door 5432 were refused in 1 ms. Door 22 got no answer, and the laptop gave up after 5 seconds. Door 8080 answered with GOOD NIGHT, HAL.

blocks.caption: Rosa drew this from my knocks. Green answered. Amber was refused at once. Red never answered at all. Door 8080 answered, just not with the program she installed.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Before anyone restarts anything, look at the box's start-up list: the programs it launches every time it powers on. And notice your laptop got two different kinds of no. One came back in a millisecond. One never came back. Those mean very different things.

replies.author: u/dell_after_hours
replies.text: Rosa says she can see the start-up list from home. She went quiet for a while after she looked.

comments.author: u/second_shift_sam
comments.text: Door 22 swallowing your knock is probably on purpose. At our place the firewall only lets in knocks on 22 from our admin's home address. Everyone else just waits until they give up.

comments.author: u/packet_ghost
comments.text: A database saying *refused* while it's clearly running is the most normal thing in this post. Ask it which address it's listening on.

reply.prompt: Rosa wants the right board running before the 5 AM drivers arrive, and she never wants this again. What should she do? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Put the new board program behind a different door, like 8081, so the two programs stop fighting over 8080.
options.part2: Rosa moved v2 to door 8081 and it started first time. Then the drivers walked in at five, looked up, and read GOOD NIGHT, HAL. The big screen still knocks on door 8080, and Hal's program was still there to answer. Two programs running, and the right one talking to nobody.
options.senior: Moving the new program to a free door makes the error go away, but every client still knocks on the old door. Find out who holds the door instead of hiding from it.

options.text: Restart the box. Whatever is running now won't survive a restart.
options.part2: I flipped the breaker again at 3 AM and counted to ten. The box came back and the screen said GOOD NIGHT, HAL. Both programs are on the start-up list, so both start with the box, and whichever grabs door 8080 first wins. Rosa says some nights v2 would win the race. Some nights isn't a fix.
options.senior: A restart clears whatever is running, but anything on the start-up list comes straight back and races for the same door. It costs minutes with no board at all, and it hides the cause.

options.text: Open every door in the firewall, so nothing is blocked while she works out what's wrong.
options.part2: Rosa opened every door. Door 22 started answering my laptop, which felt like progress. Door 8080 kept answering as Hal. And by morning the box's log was full of knocks on door 22 from all over the world, from strangers guessing passwords. The firewall was never the problem. Now it's a new one.
options.senior: The firewall only decides who gets to knock. It can't change which program answers. Open a door only to the people who need it.

options.text: Ask the box which program holds door 8080. Stop Hal's program and take it off the start-up list, start v2, then knock on 8080 and check that it's v2 answering.
options.part2: Rosa logged in at 3:40. One command named the program holding door 8080: Hal's, started by the start-up list at 1:12. She stopped it, took it off the list, and started v2. I knocked on 8080 from the laptop. It answered ORDER BOARD v2. At five the drivers read today's pickups. One thing Rosa hasn't explained yet. Every night at 2:13, the box's log shows a single knock on door 8080 from 127.0.0.1. From inside the box itself. Nobody else has a key to that closet.
options.senior: Never guess who's behind a door. Ask the machine which program holds the port, fix what starts at power-on so the right one wins every time, and check what answers, not just that something did.

sim.title: Knock on the box's doors
sim.lede: You're Dell, with Rosa's laptop. Each door on the box is a port, and each knock is a client asking a server program to answer. The clock runs 2 times faster than real life, so a knock that gets no answer waits 5 seconds of clock time, then gives up. Click any box to see what it does.
sim.tryThis: Try this: knock on 443, then 80, then 22, and compare how each one fails or answers. Knock on 5432 from the laptop, then from inside the box (localhost). Then pick 8080 and press Start: the door is already in use. Stop Hal's program, start v2 and knock again. Let outsiders in on door 22 and knock. Finally, press Restart a few times: the start-up list launches Hal's v1 and v2 in a random order, and whichever asks first gets door 8080. Take Hal's v1 off the start-up list and restart once more.

explain.oneLine: Nothing haunted the board. When the box powered back on, Hal's old program grabbed door 8080 first, so Rosa's new one couldn't start, and every knock on 8080 got Hal's answer.

steps.title: A server is a program waiting behind a door.
steps.text: A server isn't really a machine. It's a program that asks the operating system for a port, a number from 0 to 65535, and then waits for knocks on it. That waiting is called listening. A client is the program that knocks, like the screen by the lifts or Dell's laptop. One machine, with one IP address, can run many servers, each behind its own port, the way one building has many doors.

steps.title: Some doors have standard numbers.
steps.text: So clients know where to knock, common services use well-known ports, listed in a registry kept by IANA: 80 for web pages, 443 for web pages over an encrypted connection, 22 for SSH (logging in to a machine from far away) and 5432 for the PostgreSQL database. Ports 0 to 1023 are the system ports. Higher numbers like 8080 are common picks for a team's own programs.

steps.title: A knock gets one of three answers.
steps.text: Answered: a program is listening, and the conversation starts. Refused: the machine is there, but nothing listens on that port, so its operating system answers *nobody here* at once, in about a millisecond. Timed out: nothing comes back at all, usually because a firewall dropped the knock without a word, so the client waits until it gives up. Refused means you reached an empty door. Timed out means you may never have reached the door.

steps.title: Localhost is the box knocking on itself.
steps.text: 127.0.0.1, also called localhost, is the loopback address: a knock sent to it never leaves the machine. The PostgreSQL database on the box listens only on localhost, which is its default. Programs on the box can reach it. A knock from Dell's laptop arrives on the box's other address, finds nobody listening there, and is refused. That's a safety setting, not a fault.

steps.title: Only one program can hold a door.
steps.text: Rosa replaced Hal's v1 three weeks ago, but v1 was still on the box's start-up list. When the box powered on at 1:12 AM, both programs started. v1 asked for port 8080 first and got it. A moment later v2 asked for the same port, and the operating system said no: *address already in use*, the error called EADDRINUSE. v2 quit. The screen knocks on 8080, so it got Hal's program, still greeting the man who wrote it.

diagram.aria: What was behind the doors. The wall screen knocks on door 8080, which is held by Hal's v1, started at 1:12 AM. Rosa's v2 never started because the door was already in use. Dell's laptop knocks through the firewall: knocks on door 22 are dropped, so they time out, and knocks on door 5432 are refused because the database listens only on 127.0.0.1.

notes.text: dropped: you wait, then give up

explain.caption: Clients on the left, doors and the programs behind them on the right. Hal's v1 got door 8080 first after the 1:12 AM power cut, so Rosa's v2 never started. The firewall drops outside knocks on door 22, and the database listens only on 127.0.0.1, so a knock on 5432 from outside finds nobody.

fix.title: The fix: find who holds the door, then fix what starts
fix.text: Ask the machine which program holds the port. On Linux, the commands ss -ltnp or lsof -i :8080 list each listening port and the program behind it. Stop the wrong program and take it off the start-up list, so the next power cut can't bring it back. Start the right one, then knock from outside and check *who* answers, for example with a status page where each version reports its own name. Finally, make a failed start loud: a program that can't get its port should alert someone, not quietly quit while an old one keeps answering.

limits: A knock only proves that something answered. A health check that asks the program for its name and version catches the wrong program on the right door. A bare knock doesn't.
A firewall decides who may knock, not who answers. Opening doors to chase a problem usually creates a new one: an open door 22 or 5432 soon gets password-guessing knocks from all over the internet.
Refused versus timed out is a strong hint, not proof. Some firewalls send *refused* on purpose instead of staying silent, and a machine that is switched off or badly overloaded can also time out.

head: Unwanted knock
Good
Bad
rows: Tells a stranger nothing. Scanning the machine is slow and painful.
Your own mistakes look like dead machines: clients hang until they give up.
Clients fail fast with a clear answer.
Confirms to anyone who knocks that the machine is there.
Only the people who need a door can reach it. This is AWS's advice for door 22.
Needs updating when someone's address changes, which home internet does often.

explain.seniorTake: A port is a promise that one program is listening. When a client gets the wrong answer, don't stop at whether something answered. Ask *what* answered, and why that program got the door first.

realWorld.title: AWS security groups are firewalls written as rules
realWorld.text: On AWS, an EC2 server sits behind a security group, which AWS describes as a virtual firewall. Each inbound rule names a port, such as 22, and who may knock on it. Rules can only allow traffic, never deny it, and a new security group starts with no inbound rules at all, so nothing gets in until you add one. Security groups are also stateful: the answer to an allowed knock is let back out automatically. For doors 22 and 3389, AWS advises allowing only specific address ranges, never the whole internet.

realWorld.title: AWS's first suspect for Connection timed out
realWorld.text: AWS's guide to EC2 connection problems has a section for the error *Connection timed out*, and its first step is the same suspect as door 22 in this story: check the security group. You need a rule that allows inbound traffic from your computer's public IPv4 address on the right port, such as 22 for SSH. The guide also warns that a rule allowing one address stops matching when that address changes, which is common on home internet. And if your computer is on a corporate network, it says to ask the network administrator whether the office's own firewall lets that traffic through.

realWorld.title: PostgreSQL listens on localhost unless told otherwise
realWorld.text: PostgreSQL's documentation gives its default port as 5432 and its default listen address as localhost, which allows only loopback connections from the same machine. A fresh database refuses knocks from every other machine until someone changes that setting on purpose. Door 5432 in this story was the safe default doing its job.

asked: What's the difference between connection refused and connection timed out?
Your service works on your laptop, but other machines can't reach it. Where do you look?
interview.answer: Refused means the machine was reached and its operating system said nothing listens on that port, so check that the program is running, and on which port and address. Timed out means nothing came back: usually a firewall or security group dropping the traffic, sometimes a wrong address or a dead or overloaded machine. For works-on-my-laptop, check the address the program listens on (localhost only is a common default), then the port, then the firewall or security group rule for that port and source. Test from inside the machine and from outside to see which layer fails. If a program won't start with address already in use, find the program holding the port before picking a new one.

terms.def: A number from 0 to 65535 that picks one door on a machine. The IP address finds the building, the port finds the door. Each listening program holds its own port.
A program that asks for a port and waits for clients to knock on it. People also call the machine it runs on a server, but the program is what answers.
A program that knocks on a server's port and asks for something, like a browser, a phone app, or the order board screen.
What a server program does while it waits on its port for clients to connect.
This story's word for a connection attempt: a client trying to reach a program on one port of one machine.
An open line between a client and a server program, made when a knock is answered. Requests and answers travel over it.
A standard port number for a common service, so clients know where to knock: 80 for web pages, 443 for encrypted web pages, 22 for SSH, 5432 for PostgreSQL.
Ports 0 to 1023, the range IANA keeps for the most common services.
Internet Assigned Numbers Authority: the body that keeps the official lists of internet numbers, including which service uses which port.
A server program that sends web pages to browsers. It usually listens on port 80, or 443 for the encrypted kind.
A connection scrambled so only the two ends can read it. Web pages over port 443 use one. A later case covers how it works.
Secure Shell: a way to log in to a machine from far away and type commands on it. It listens on port 22.
A program that stores data and answers questions about it, like the list of today's pickups.
A popular free database, often called Postgres. It listens on port 5432 and, by default, only on localhost.
The name a machine uses for itself. Knocks sent to localhost never leave the machine. It means the same as 127.0.0.1.
The loopback address: an IP address that always means this same machine. Traffic sent to it stays inside.
An address that loops straight back to the machine that used it, like 127.0.0.1. Addresses starting with 127 must never leave the machine.
Which of a machine's addresses a program answers on. Listening on localhost only means outside machines are refused.
A guard in front of a machine's ports that decides which knocks get through, usually by port and by who is knocking. Knocks it blocks are often dropped without a reply.
The answer when a knock reaches the machine but nothing listens on that port. It comes back at once. On Linux the error is called ECONNREFUSED.
What happens when a knock gets no answer at all and the client stops waiting. Often a firewall dropped it. On Linux the error is called ETIMEDOUT.
The error a program gets when it asks for a port another program already holds. On Linux it's called EADDRINUSE. Only one program can hold a port.
The operating system's short name for address already in use: the port you asked for is taken.
The programs a machine launches by itself every time it powers on. A program left on it comes back after every restart.
Switching a machine or program off and on again. Everything running stops, and whatever is on the start-up list starts again.
The switch in a building's power box that cuts the power when a circuit is overloaded.
Version 1, version 2: the first and second release of a program.
A thousandth of a second, written ms.
A free operating system that runs most of the world's servers.
Linux commands that list which ports have a program listening and which program it is.
An automatic test that asks a program whether it's working, and ideally which version it is.
A simple page a program serves about itself, such as its name, version and whether it's healthy.
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud: AWS's service for renting servers by the hour. Each rented server is called an instance.
One server you rent from EC2.
AWS's built-in firewall for EC2 instances. Its rules list which ports may be reached, and from which addresses. It can only allow, never deny.
A security group rule for traffic coming in: which port, and which source addresses are allowed to knock on it.
For a firewall: it remembers allowed connections, so the replies to them get through without a separate rule.
The IP address the rest of the internet sees for your home or office connection. IPv4 is the familiar four-number style, like 203.0.113.7. Home ones often change.
The port for Windows Remote Desktop, the Windows way to log in from far away. Like 22, it attracts password guessing.
In a firewall or security group rule, every IPv4 address there is: the whole internet.

atWork: Open the EC2 console in your AWS account (read-only access is enough) and pick one instance. On its Security tab, read the inbound rules. For each rule, write down the port, which program should be listening behind it, and who the source lets knock. Flag any rule for port 22 or a database port like 5432 whose source is 0.0.0.0/0, the whole internet. Then, on a machine you're allowed to log in to, list the listening ports (ss -ltnp on Linux) and check two things: every port open in the rules has the program you expect behind it, and every listening program has a reason to be there.

recall.prompt: You start your app and it quits with address already in use on port 8080. A coworker says: just use 8081. What do you do instead, and why?

keyIdeas.idea: Find out which program holds port 8080
Clients still knock on 8080 and get the old program
Stop it and fix what starts it, so it can't come back

recall.model: Don't move. Every client still knocks on 8080, so they'd keep getting whatever holds it now. Ask the machine which program has the port (ss -ltnp or lsof -i :8080), work out why it's running (often an old version still on the start-up list), stop it and remove it from whatever starts it, then start yours and check from outside that your program is the one answering.

recall.prompt: From your laptop, a knock on a server's port 5432 comes back refused in 1 ms. The database is definitely running. What's the most likely reason?
options: A firewall is dropping the knock
The database listens only on localhost, so nothing listens on the address you knocked on
Port 5432 is too high a number to reach from outside
recall.why: A refusal in a millisecond means the machine answered: it's on, and the knock got through. Nothing was listening on that address and port. PostgreSQL listens only on localhost by default.

recall.prompt: On the same machine, a knock on port 22 gets no answer and gives up after 5 seconds, while a knock on port 80 is refused in 1 ms. What does that tell you?
options: The machine is reachable, and something like a firewall is silently dropping knocks on port 22
The program on port 22 is just slow today
recall.why: The fast refusal on 80 proves the machine is up and reachable. Silence on 22 means the knock never got an answer at all, which is what a firewall or security group dropping it looks like.

recall.prompt: Your team launches a new EC2 instance running a web server on port 443. From home, the browser spins and then says the connection timed out. On the instance itself, a knock on localhost port 443 is answered. Where's the problem, and what do you check?

keyIdeas.idea: The program is fine: it answers from inside
A timeout points at the security group or firewall
The rule must allow port 443 from the right source

recall.model: The web server is running and listening, because the knock from inside the instance was answered. A timeout from outside means the knock was dropped on the way, so check the instance's security group: it needs an inbound rule for port 443 from the people who should reach it (for a public website, 0.0.0.0/0). If there's also a firewall on the instance itself, check that it allows 443 too.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 4 months later. Rosa moved the order board to a new EC2 instance on AWS. It works from her laptop at home. From the office, the screen by the lifts spins and then says *connection timed out*. On the instance itself, a knock on localhost port 8080 answers ORDER BOARD v2. Rosa's plan for tonight: open every port in the security group to 0.0.0.0/0, just to see.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What's actually wrong, and what should Rosa do instead?

keyIdeas.idea: The program is fine: it answered on localhost and works from her home
A timeout means something on the way drops the office's knocks on 8080: the security group or the office's own firewall
Allow port 8080 from the office's address only, not everything

coldCase.model: The board program is fine: it answers on localhost and from Rosa's home. A timeout from the office means the knock was dropped on the way. The most likely suspects are the security group, which may allow 8080 only from Rosa's home address, or the office's own firewall, which may block outgoing knocks on 8080. Test from a third network, like a phone's mobile data. If that times out too, the security group only lets Rosa's home in: add one inbound rule for port 8080 with the office's public address as the source. If it works, the security group is fine and the office firewall is the guard, so ask whoever runs it. Either way, don't open every port to the internet. Knock from the office to check, and leave everything else closed.
